items.title: Headlines for October 26, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won reelection, defeating far-right challenger Flávio Bolsonaro. Lula won with nearly 51.8% of the ballot, a difference of more than 4 million votes. Bolsonaro quickly rejected the outcome, saying he would ask a court to annul the result. Lula’s victory marked a stunning reversal from a first round of voting three weeks ago, when he trailed Bolsonaro by over 2 million votes. President Lula spoke to supporters after polls closed Sunday evening. ... In Serbia, longtime leader Aleksandar Vučić has conceded defeat, after an election that pitted him against a student-led movement calling for an end to corruption, mass surveillance, political violence and democratic backsliding. Vučić conceded after early results showed the opposition Student List poised to win more than 135 seats in the 250-member parliament, compared with 105 for Vučić’s list. It’s a historic victory for the student-led movement that rose up in November 2024 in response to the collapse of a roof at a train station in the city of Novi Sad, which killed 16 people. The disaster became a focal point for protests over government corruption and inefficiency. This is opposition candidate Radomir Saičić speaking after Sunday’s election. ... ## French Police Arrest More Than 1,300 People During Saturday Protests ... In France, police arrested more than 1,300 people Saturday as hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets for another day of protests demanding better schools and relief from the soaring cost of living. The protests came despite a decree by President Emmanuel Macron earlier in the week that outlawed public demonstrations except those by recognized trade unions. Hundreds of people were jailed after fast-track court proceedings. This is a protester at Saturday’s rally in Paris, where organizers estimate a quarter of a million people marched.

items.excerpt: The inflation data this week produced a trifecta of upside surprises, starting with the consumer price index on Wednesday, producer price index on Thursday, and (to a much lesser extent) import prices on Friday. This briefly pushed rate hike expectations for the October 28 meeting to almost 50% before turbulence in financial markets helped bring that down to 15% Friday morning. Consumer prices rose 0.6% MoM in September, driven heavily by a 9.1% MoM jump in gasoline prices that lifted the energy complex by 5.2% MoM. By contrast, food prices were unchanged, which is good news but unlikely to last. Overall goods prices rose a brisk 1.2% (double the August pace) and are now up 4.6% YoY. Services prices rose 0.4% MoM and are up 3.2% YoY. Within services, airfares posted another sizable gain and are 22.4% higher than a year earlier; this is where the energy price shock is unmistakable. The report’s most troubling development was a 0.4% monthly increase in shelter costs. Apart from an anomalous reading in April, this was the largest increase since August 2024 and the clearest blemish in the report. There were some mitigating details. Hotel rates inflated the category, while rent of primary residence rose by a more modest 0.2%. Even so, a meaningful slowdown next month will be needed to ease concerns that the shelter disinflation process has stalled or ended. All these lifted the headline inflation rate three tenths to 3.7% YoY and the core rate two tenths to 2.6% YoY. At higher precision, the two numbers were 3.738% and 2.564%, respectively. Producer prices surged 1.3% MoM, lifting the YoY comparison to 6.3%, the highest reading since December 2022. Goods PPI inflation accelerated 2.2 percentage points (ppt) to 9.8% YoY, and services PPI inflation accelerated 0.2 (ppt) to 4.9% YoY. Both core metrics (ex-food and energy; and ex-food, energy, and trade services) advanced two tenths to 5.0% YoY. items.title: Trump promised to stop inflation. Now Republicans may ...
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump would prefer that voters not worry about inflation. But it's hard for them to ignore. Filling up a basic Ford F-150 truck now costs about $100, up $30 from a year ago. Mortgage rates have jumped to levels that have depressed home sales. And for the past 12 months, consumer prices have risen faster than paychecks, making the average family poorer. One week before midterm elections that will serve as a referendum on his second term, Trump is struggling to deliver on his campaign promise to bring down costs, even as he insists the country has entered an economic "golden age." The same frustration that powered his comeback two years ago could now cost Republicans control of Congress. "Our nation is doing better now than ever before," Trump insists while campaigning, vowing that interest rates and oil prices will plunge once the war with Iran — which he started — comes to an end. The word "affordability," he says, is nothing but "a con job by the Democrats," adding that "it doesn't mean anything to anybody." ... That rhetoric comes as voters say they're struggling to afford basics like fuel and groceries and as they blame Trump for higher costs, pointing to the Republican president's aggressive tariff policies and the ongoing, unpopular war with Iran. Record-high diesel prices, in particular, have driven up shipping and farming costs, creating trouble for Republicans in typically conservative states such as Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas, where Democrats appear uniquely competitive in races that will shape Trump's final two years in office. "The costs of things are absolutely the first thing people talk about, but also it's their pay not keeping up with the cost," said AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler. "It's a double whammy."

items.excerpt: 'You Can See Everything' surges with $19.5M at box office; 'Clayface' takes No. 1 ... NEW YORK (AP) — DC Studios scored a modest, R-rated win with “Clayface,” landing a $24 million opening weekend, according to studio estimates Sunday. But the biggest success story in theaters remained A24’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything,” which pulled in $19.5 million in its first weekend of wide release. The Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim-directed “You Can See Everything” increased from 855 locations to 2,655. In expansion, it continued to blow away expectations. With $45.1 million in two weeks, it already ranks among the highest grossing documentaries ever. Ticket sales were also good for the stop motion animation “Wildwood” and the comic fable “Wicker.” But “Ali G: Who Iz I?” was a nonevent in cinemas.

items.title: Tokyo Film Festival to Open With Zeze Takahisa's Sukiyaki
items.excerpt: The 39th edition Tokyo International Film Festival (TIFF) will open on Oct. 26 with a gala screening of Zeze Takahisa’s music drama Sukiyaki. Festival organizers also revealed that Yeon Sang-ho‘s zombie action horror film Colony will close this year’s event on Nov. 4. Based on true events, Sukiyaki tells the story behind the famed Japanese pop song “Sukiyaki,” sung by crooner Kyu Sakamoto. The song topped the charts in a forward-looking post-war Japan but remarkably became a global phenomenon, holding the No.1 spot on U.S. Billboard charts for three consecutive weeks in 1963. The film, which is a sure-fire bet to be a hit when it opens in Japanese theaters on Dec. 25, depicts the history-making collaboration between the song’s composer Nakamura Hachidai (Okada Junichi), lyricist Ei Rokusuke (Matsuzaka Tori), and Sakamoto (Nakano Taiga). ... “ Sukiyaki tells the dramatic stories of three artists who inspired people in postwar Japan, interwoven with a collection of musical masterpieces. We are delighted to open the festival with this moving film, which stars three of today’s most prominent Japanese actors,” said Ichiyama Shozo, TIFF’s programming director. ... TIFF’s closing film this year will be the wonderfully inventive Korean zombie film Colony, that that wowed genre fans when it premiered in the Midnight Screenings section of the Cannes Film Festival earlier this year. The film tells the story of a biological weapon being unleashed inside a Seoul skyscraper that turns the people trapped inside the building into a deadly zombie hive mind. Colony was a huge hit when it was released in South Korean cinemas and won plaudits from critics. The movie comes from Yeon, the director behind Korean classics such as Train to Busan, Seoul Station and Peninsula. The prolific filmmaker also created the hit Netflix shows Hellbound and Parasyte: The Grey. ... Additionally, TIFF has also announced that it will screen Takashi Yamazaki‘s Godzilla Minus Zero as a special Centerpiece screening at the festival. The hotly anticipated film, a followup to the Oscar-winning global box office smash Godzilla Minus One, has the distinction of being the first Japanese production to be filmed for Imax. The logline for the film reads, “War reduced Japan to zero, and Godzilla plunged it even further, into minus territory. Two yearshave passed since then, and the country has faced agonizing struggles to achieve recovery andfinally return to normalcy. But just as humanity is clinging to a hard-won peace, a new threatstrikes, crushing hope in an instant.” ... TIFF 2026 runs from Oct. 26 through to Nov. 4.
